name: Abbey Road Studios
description: The most famous recording studio in the world — EMI's St John's Wood studio where The Beatles recorded 11 of their 13 albums, and where Adele, Radiohead, Kanye, and Oasis have also recorded.
tips: Free exterior visit. The Abbey Road Shop next door sells merch — the only way inside the building without being a recording artist.

name: Abbey Road Zebra Crossing
description: The most famous crossing in the world, photographed for The Beatles' Abbey Road album cover on 8 August 1969. Grade II-listed.
tips: Live-streamed 24/7 by the Abbey Road webcam. Morning is quieter. Do NOT actually stop in the middle — drivers are used to tourists but it's a working road.

name: 3 Savile Row (Apple Corps Rooftop)
description: The rooftop where The Beatles played their final live performance on 30 January 1969 — a 42-minute gig that stopped Savile Row. Site of Apple Corps HQ.
tips: Private office — exterior only. The plaque is subtle, look up at the roof.

name: The 100 Club
description: Oxford Street basement jazz-and-punk legend since 1942 — hosted the first Sex Pistols' performance of 'Anarchy', plus Muddy Waters, The Rolling Stones, and weekly new bands today.
tips: Saved from closure in 2010 by Paul McCartney's campaign. Cash-friendly bar.

name: Site of the Marquee Club
description: The original Marquee Club (Wardour Street, 1964-88) was London's most influential rock venue — The Who, Rolling Stones, Yes, Hendrix residencies. Building replaced but site commemorated.
tips: Blue plaque at the site. Also 165 Oxford Street (original 1958-64 location) is worth finding.

name: Cavendish Square (Amy Winehouse Statue)
description: A life-size bronze of Amy Winehouse in Camden's Stables Market — erected in 2014, on what would have been her 31st birthday.
tips: Fans leave messages at the plinth. Combine with The Dublin Castle pub where she played.

name: Café OTO
description: The UK's most important experimental-music venue — Dalston basement where free jazz, drone, improvised, and avant-garde artists play almost nightly.
tips: Daytime café, evening gigs. Excellent record/book shop upstairs.

name: The Vortex Jazz Club
description: Dalston's 100-seat contemporary-jazz club — Tuesday improv nights, Friday showcases. One of Europe's most respected intimate jazz rooms.
tips: Free-improv Tuesdays. Excellent sound.

name: Jazz Café Camden
description: Camden's 400-cap genre-spanning club — not just jazz; soul, hip-hop, funk, Afrobeat, neo-soul. Early D'Angelo, Kamasi Washington, Little Simz shows.
tips: Balcony dining tables book out. Standing is livelier.

name: Royal Festival Hall
description: Festival of Britain's 1951 modernist concert hall — London Philharmonic resident, Philharmonia, and free foyer programmes daily.
tips: Free foyer performances most days. Grade I-listed.

name: Barbican Hall
description: Home of the London Symphony Orchestra and BBC Symphony — 1,943-seat Brutalist concert hall with acoustics designed by Cyril Harris.
tips: Under-26 tickets £5-15. Pre-concert talks free with tickets.

name: The Roundhouse
description: Grade II-listed Victorian engine shed turned rock-era venue — hosted Hendrix, The Doors, Pink Floyd, and is now London's premier mid-sized music/circus venue.
tips: The Roundhouse Rising emerging-artists festival (September) is a talent-spotter's goldmine.

name: KOKO Camden
description: 1900-cap Grade II-listed former theatre — Charlie Chaplin's first performance venue, Rolling Stones filmed 'Rock and Roll Circus' here. Reopened 2022 after fire restoration.
tips: Restored ceiling is spectacular. Rooftop bar for members.

name: Eventim Apollo (Hammersmith Odeon)
description: 5,039-cap Art Deco theatre — where Bowie 'retired' Ziggy Stardust in 1973, where Queen filmed 'A Night at the Opera'. One of London's great atmospheric rooms.
tips: Seated-only venue (originally designed for cinema). Stalls middle rows are sweet spot.

name: O2 Academy Brixton
description: Grade II-listed 4,921-cap Art Deco venue (1929) — generally considered the best mid-sized rock venue in the UK. Springsteen, Dylan, Oasis, Prince all played here.
tips: Sloped floor means great views from anywhere. Closed 2022-24 after crushing incident — check reopening status.

name: Electric Ballroom Camden
description: 1,100-cap Camden rock landmark (1938) — Sid Vicious, The Clash, Public Image, U2, Joy Division, and every punk band of note played here.
tips: Saturday market runs on-site during the day.

name: Troxy
description: A 1933 Art Deco cinema turned 3,100-cap concert hall in Limehouse — hosts everything from electronic megastars to opera.
tips: Chandeliers intact. Opera gala nights worth the ticket.

name: Scala King's Cross
description: A 1920 former cinema turned 1,145-cap nightclub-venue — multi-level, late-license, a London clubbing classic and indie-gig fixture.
tips: Balcony smoking area is a London institution.

name: Lafayette
description: A King's Cross 600-cap venue + restaurant from the Omeara team — high-end sound, balcony dining, refined indie programming.
tips: Dinner-and-show tables book months ahead.

name: EartH (Evolutionary Arts Hackney)
description: A Grade II-listed 1930s Art Deco cinema turned 2,000-cap venue + restaurant + theatre — experimental programming, genuinely boundary-pushing.
tips: Multi-space venue — check which room your show's in.

name: London Coliseum (English National Opera)
description: Frank Matcham's 1904 gilded rococo theatre — home to English National Opera, with the largest theatre capacity in London (2,359).
tips: ENO performs operas in English translation. £10 under-21 tickets.

name: Trident Studios
description: 8 St Anne's Court — the Soho studio where Bowie's 'Hunky Dory', Queen's 'Bohemian Rhapsody', Elton John's 'Goodbye Yellow Brick Road', and The Beatles' 'Hey Jude' were recorded.
tips: Private working studio — exterior only. Plaque commemorates the classic recordings.

name: AIR Studios
description: George Martin's Hampstead studio in the former Lyndhurst Hall church — where classical scores for Lord of the Rings, Inception, and Harry Potter were recorded.
tips: Private studio — exterior only. Occasional open days during Open House weekend.

name: Olympic Studios
description: A Barnes cinema once home to legendary recording studios — Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil', Led Zeppelin II, Hendrix 'Electric Ladyland' recorded here. Now a cinema + café.
tips: Recording plaques throughout the café. Café-cinema combo makes for a great night out.

name: RAK Studios
description: Mickie Most's 1976 studio near Abbey Road — where Kim Wilde, Duran Duran, Bananarama, Adele, Radiohead, and Arctic Monkeys have recorded.
tips: Private studio. Walk from Abbey Road — 5 minutes between them.

name: Strongroom Studios
description: Shoreditch complex of 14 studios — Spice Girls, Arctic Monkeys, Björk, Gorillaz, Wolf Alice have recorded here. Public bar on-site.
tips: Strongroom Bar is open to the public — go for a drink, see which acts are in.

name: Metropolis Studios
description: Chiswick Power Station turned recording complex — Michael Jackson, Queen, Amy Winehouse, Lady Gaga, Adele all have recorded here.
address: The Power House, 70 Chiswick High Rd, London W4 1SY
tips: Private studio — exterior visible from the street.

name: Eastcote Studios
description: Kilburn recording studio since 1978 — Adele's 21, PJ Harvey, Depeche Mode, The Verve. Quiet, unpretentious, beloved by artists.
tips: Exterior only.

name: Denmark Street (Tin Pan Alley)
description: A tiny Soho street that was the heart of the UK music industry 1960s-90s — Sex Pistols lived at No. 6, Elton John wrote 'Your Song' at No. 20, The Rolling Stones recorded their first demo here.
tips: Guitar shops still line the street. Bob Marley recorded his first UK sessions here.

name: Heddon Street (Ziggy Stardust Location)
description: The narrow Mayfair alley where Bowie was photographed for the cover of 'The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars' (1972). Plaque marks the spot.
tips: Now a dining courtyard. Plaque installed 2012. K.West sign was reconstructed.

name: David Bowie Mural Brixton
description: Jimmy C's 2013 Aladdin Sane-era mural opposite Brixton Tube — became an impromptu shrine after Bowie's death in 2016. Now officially protected.
tips: Bowie was born in Brixton. Fans still leave flowers and messages.

name: Camden Stables Statue of Amy Winehouse
description: A life-size bronze of Amy Winehouse — erected in 2014 on what would have been her 31st birthday, in Camden Stables Market.
address: Camden Stables Market, Chalk Farm Rd, London NW1 8AH
tips: Pair with The Hawley Arms pub (Chalk Farm Road) — her favourite local.

name: Freddie Mercury's House (Garden Lodge)
description: Freddie Mercury's Kensington home 1980-91 — a green wall covered with fans' messages since his death. Still privately owned; a pilgrimage site.
tips: Respect neighbours — fans have been messaging the wall since 1991. Don't knock.

name: Joe Strummer Mural (Ladbroke Grove)
description: Graffiti portrait of The Clash's Joe Strummer on a West London subway wall — a working-class memorial, frequently refreshed by fans.
tips: Strummer's Notting Hill roots. Combine with Portobello Road walk.

name: Haddon Hall, Beckenham (Bowie's Flat)
description: The Beckenham flat where David Bowie wrote 'Ziggy Stardust' and 'Hunky Dory' — Grade II-listed detached Victorian, now privately owned. Exterior visit only.
tips: 30 min train from Victoria. Blue plaque at the gate.

name: 34 Montagu Square (Lennon/Yoko Flat)
description: John Lennon and Yoko Ono's 1968 flat — where they were famously arrested for drugs, and where Ringo Starr, Hendrix, and Paul McCartney also once lived.
tips: Private flat — blue plaque outside. Hendrix recorded demos here.

name: 7 Cavendish Avenue (McCartney Home)
description: Paul McCartney's St John's Wood home since 1965 — where the final touches to Sgt Pepper's and Abbey Road were done. Still his London residence today.
tips: Private residence — respect. Around the corner from Abbey Road.

name: Hyde Park (Rolling Stones 1969)
description: The open-air site of The Rolling Stones' free concert on 5 July 1969 — attended by 250,000, two days after Brian Jones's death. Bob Dylan, Queen, and BST festival have since played here.
tips: BST Hyde Park summer festival holds the same stage tradition.

name: Battersea Power Station (Pink Floyd Album Cover)
description: The iconic 1933 power station featured on the cover of Pink Floyd's 1977 album 'Animals' — inflatable pig originally floated over the chimneys.
tips: Now a mixed-use development — shops, restaurants, and a viewing lift up one of the chimneys (£15).

name: Rainbow Theatre (Finsbury Park)
description: Former 1930 Art Deco cinema turned rock venue (1971-82) — Hendrix, The Who, Led Zeppelin, Bob Marley, Pink Floyd all played here. Now a Brazilian Pentecostal church.
tips: Exterior Grade II*-listed. Occasional open days.

name: The Roxy Club Site
description: 41-43 Neal Street — the Covent Garden venue (1976-78) that hosted the first Sex Pistols gig, The Damned, Generation X, The Clash. A punk Ground Zero.
tips: Now a fashion retailer. Plaque commemorates The Clash's first show.

name: Virgin Records Original Store
description: Richard Branson's original Virgin record shop (1971) — 15-19 South Wharf Road near Paddington. The first retail step before the label.
tips: Second flagship at 24 Oxford Street 1976 was equally legendary.

name: Rough Trade West
description: The original 1976 Rough Trade in Notting Hill — smaller and more specialist, the root of the Rough Trade label (The Smiths, The Strokes).
tips: Second-hand dig-crate heaven. Portobello Road nearby.

name: Sister Ray Records
description: Soho's longest-serving independent record shop (1987) — broad, knowledgeable, strong on electronic, punk, and alternative.
tips: Second-hand section upstairs.

name: Sounds of the Universe
description: Berwick Street specialist record shop — linked to Soul Jazz label, focused on reggae, soul, jazz, funk, and African music.
tips: Soul Jazz reissues curated on the ground floor.

name: Phonica Records
description: Poland Street specialist in house, techno, disco, and electronica — Europe's most respected DJ record shop.
tips: Listening decks available. Phonica label releases stocked.

name: Honest Jon's
description: Portobello Road specialist since 1974 — reggae, jazz, African, Latin, global music. Damon Albarn's label home; impeccable curation.
tips: Saturday market day busiest. Listening decks.

name: Reckless Records
description: Berwick Street's second-hand-focused store since 1984 — rare records, fair prices, a London vinyl-collector's regular haunt.
tips: Bring your own unwanted vinyl — they buy.

name: Flashback Records
description: Three-branch London second-hand specialist (Islington, Crouch End, Shoreditch) — huge stock, strong vintage, frequent bargains.
tips: Crouch End branch has the best jazz selection; Shoreditch for newer releases.

name: Kristina Records
description: Dalston specialist run by ex-Rough Trade staff — post-punk, electronic, krautrock, jazz. Small, sharp, seriously curated.
tips: Tiny — squeeze in past the door.

name: Love Vinyl
description: Hoxton specialist in house, disco, techno, and soul — a warm DJ-culture shop run by and for crate-diggers.
tips: In-store DJ sets Friday evenings.

name: All Ages Records
description: Camden Town punk and hardcore specialist since 2003 — the only London shop dedicated to hardcore, DIY, and contemporary punk scenes.
tips: Frequent in-store gigs — check calendar.

name: BBC Proms
description: Eight weeks of world-class classical music at the Royal Albert Hall (July-September) — the largest classical music festival in the world.
address: Royal Albert Hall, Kensington Gore, London SW7 2AP
tips: 'Promenading' standing tickets £8 on the day — queue from 11am. Last Night is iconic.

name: EFG London Jazz Festival
description: 10-day November festival spanning 60+ venues across London — from Ronnie Scott's to free lunchtime concerts. The biggest UK jazz festival.
tips: Free events at Southbank Centre. Mid-November dates.

name: Field Day Festival
description: One-day electronic-and-indie festival (June) in Brockwell Park — lineups span techno, house, pop, and alternative acts.
tips: Combine with Cross the Tracks (following day) for a jazz-soul-funk sister event.

name: Cross the Tracks Festival
description: Brockwell Park's jazz, funk, soul, and reggae festival (late May) — featured Nile Rodgers, Kamasi Washington, Craig Charles.
tips: Family-friendly. Arrive early for sound-system sets.

name: Mighty Hoopla
description: Pop-focused one-day festival (June) in Brockwell Park — a celebration of LGBT+ pop icons and 90s/00s nostalgia.
tips: Costumes encouraged. Saturdays sell out fast.

name: All Points East
description: Victoria Park's 10-day indie-and-alternative summer festival (May/June) — LCD Soundsystem, The Strokes, Arctic Monkeys have headlined.
tips: Free 'In the Neighbourhood' Wed-Thu days.

name: Wireless Festival
description: Europe's biggest urban-music festival (July) — hip-hop, R&B, Afrobeats, rap. Drake, Cardi B, Travis Scott, Stormzy have headlined.
tips: Three-day passes cheapest.

name: British Summer Time Hyde Park
description: Hyde Park's headline summer concert series (early July) — Springsteen, Billy Joel, Paul McCartney, Adele, and others across two weekends.
tips: Open House midweek days are free — smaller acts in the park.

name: Lovebox Festival
description: Gunnersbury Park's electronic/hip-hop festival (mid-July) — Chase & Status, Frank Ocean, Solange, Skepta have headlined.
tips: Sister festival Citadel (family-friendly) runs the following day.

name: Meltdown Festival
description: Southbank Centre's annual curated festival (late May-June) — past curators Bowie, Morrissey, Björk, Robert Smith, Patti Smith, Grace Jones.
address: Southbank Centre, Belvedere Rd, London SE1 8XX
tips: Who curates changes annually — an indicator of that year's programme.

name: City Splash Festival
description: Reggae and Caribbean music festival (late May) — sound systems, live acts, family-friendly, Brixton's own celebration.
tips: Family-friendly. Sound-system rigs are the draw.

name: Notting Hill Carnival Sound Systems
description: Europe's biggest street festival (late August bank holiday) — 35+ static sound systems pumping reggae, dub, soca, dancehall across two days.
tips: Sunday is family-focused; Monday is the big parade. Channel One, King Tubby's Hi-Fi, Aba Shanti-I are legendary rigs.

name: South West Four
description: Clapham Common's annual dance-music festival (late August bank holiday) — trance, techno, house, drum & bass.
tips: Weekend tickets. Bank-holiday Monday.

name: St Martin-in-the-Fields Lunchtime Concerts
description: Free classical concerts Monday, Tuesday, and Friday at 1pm — 45 minutes in Gibbs's 1726 neoclassical church.
tips: Free, suggested donation. Evening candlelit concerts (£15-30) also excellent.

name: Evensong at St Paul's Cathedral
description: Daily (except Wednesday) 17:00 sung Evensong — the St Paul's Cathedral Choir, in the Wren dome, with acoustics that transform the experience.
tips: Free (no cathedral entry fee for Evensong). One of London's great musical rituals.

name: Evensong at Westminster Abbey
description: Weekday Evensong (17:00) at Westminster Abbey — the Abbey Choir, polyphony at its most exquisite, free with no Abbey entry fee.
tips: Arrive 16:40. Sit in the quire stalls if allowed.

name: St John's Smith Square
description: Thomas Archer's 1728 English Baroque church turned classical-music venue — superb acoustics for chamber, choral, and early music.
tips: Also known as 'Queen Anne's footstool' for its four-corner towers.

name: Milton Court Concert Hall
description: Guildhall School of Music's 608-seat purpose-built concert hall next to the Barbican — student performances are often world-class and cheap.
tips: Student concerts often free — check website.

name: Royal Academy of Music Museum
description: Britain's oldest music conservatoire (1822) — free museum of historic instruments, manuscripts, and recordings by Menuhin, Elton John, and more.
tips: Free. Student recitals also free — check website.

name: Royal College of Music Museum
description: Royal College of Music's free museum — 800 instruments from 15th century to present, including the world's oldest surviving guitar (1567).
tips: Free. Student recitals also frequently free.

name: Horniman Museum Music Gallery
description: One of the UK's finest collections of musical instruments — 1,300 instruments from 6 continents, with interactive listening posts.
tips: Free. Family-friendly interactive stations.

name: V&A Theatre & Performance Collection
description: The V&A's free permanent gallery dedicated to UK performing arts — iconic Bowie, Elton, Kate Bush costumes, Swinging 60s memorabilia.
tips: Free. Includes the ceremonial Olivier Award and music-industry archives.

name: British Library Sound Archive
description: The UK's national sound archive — 7 million recordings, with public 'Sounds' listening booths inside the library, free to use.
tips: Free to use. Book a listening booth at the information desk.

name: The Beatles Store
description: Baker Street's official Beatles memorabilia store — walls of rare photographs, limited vinyl, replica instruments, the biggest Beatles retail in London.
tips: Free to browse. Combine with Sherlock Holmes Museum next door.

name: Fender London
description: Fender Europe's flagship store and try-out showroom — more Fender guitars than anywhere else in Europe, live amps to play through.
address: Tottenham Ct Rd area, London W1T
tips: Free to try any guitar — bring your own picks.

name: The George Tavern
description: A 17th-century Stepney pub with a 180-cap basement venue — Amy Winehouse played here; experimental and indie programming today.
tips: Save-the-George campaign saved it from demolition. Support the venue.

name: The Hope & Anchor
description: Islington's pub-rock shrine since 1975 — Joy Division, U2, The Specials, Madness all played here early in their careers.
tips: Basement venue, 70-cap. Gigs most nights.

name: Drumsheds (Printworks successor)
description: A vast Tottenham ex-industrial venue — Broadwick Live's successor to Printworks, with 15,000+ capacity electronic events.
tips: Meridian Water station. Check event calendar.

name: Denmark Street Heritage Walk
description: Self-guided walk along Tin Pan Alley — pointing out the flats, offices, and shops of Elton John, David Bowie, Sex Pistols, The Rolling Stones.
tips: Plaques along the street. No. 6 was Sex Pistols' flat; No. 20 where Elton John wrote Your Song.

name: Trinity Laban Conservatoire
description: Daniel Libeskind's Laban Building in Deptford — the UK's biggest contemporary dance and music conservatoire. Student concerts are often free.
tips: Student showcases frequently free. Blackheath Halls is associated.

name: Regent Street Cinema Silent Film Concerts
description: The cinema where the Lumière brothers first screened to the UK public (1896) — regular silent-film-with-live-orchestra concerts.
tips: Only cinema in London still projecting 35mm regularly.

name: Carnaby Street (Swinging 60s)
description: The heart of Swinging London — where The Who, The Small Faces, and the Mod scene converged. Original boutiques mostly gone but plaques mark the history.
tips: Christmas lights installation famously music-themed each year.

name: Apple Boutique Site (94 Baker St)
description: The Beatles' short-lived 1967 psychedelic clothing boutique — original murals painted by Dutch collective The Fool; closed after 7 months.
tips: Now a different shop — plaque outside.

name: Marc Bolan's Tree
description: The tree in Barnes where Marc Bolan (T. Rex) died in a car crash on 16 September 1977 — now a bronze-plaqued shrine.
tips: Fans still leave tributes. Anniversary vigils draw crowds.

name: Handel & Hendrix in London
description: Two legendary musicians 200 years apart lived in adjoining Mayfair houses — Handel at No. 25 (1723-1759), Hendrix at No. 23 (1968-69). Both preserved as museum homes.
tips: Hendrix's flat restored to 1969 — his guitars, album collection, and ashtrays exactly where he left them.

name: Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club
description: London's most legendary jazz club, open since 1959 — Miles Davis, Ella Fitzgerald, Chet Baker and countless giants have played this Frith Street basement.
tips: Late show (11:30pm) cheaper than main show. Dinner tables best for view.

name: Royal Albert Hall
description: Victorian domed concert hall (1871) — home of the BBC Proms, site of Hendrix's 1969 gig, Cream's farewell, Adele's live album, and countless classical landmarks.
tips: Proms standing tickets £8 on the day. Daytime tours £18.

name: Wigmore Hall
description: One of the world's finest chamber-music recital halls (1901) — 552 seats under a painted cupola, Arts and Crafts decor, legendary acoustics.
tips: Sunday coffee concerts £20 — best value in classical London.

name: Union Chapel
description: Working 1877 Gothic chapel that doubles as London's most beautiful 900-cap music venue — stained glass, pews, extraordinary acoustics.
tips: Pew seating — arrive early for front rows. Daytime Sanctuary Series is free.

name: The Dublin Castle
description: Camden pub where Madness broke through and where Amy Winehouse later held court — 180-cap back room still hosts nightly new-band gigs.
tips: Cash-only. Gigs nightly £5-10.

name: Windmill Brixton
description: Tiny 80-cap Brixton pub-venue that launched Fat White Family, shame, Black Country New Road — incubator of London's post-punk revival.
tips: Cash-friendly. Frequent sell-outs — arrive early.

name: The Good Mixer
description: Camden's Britpop shrine — Blur, Oasis, Pulp, Elastica all drank here in the 1990s. Unchanged pub, jukebox, pool table.
tips: Famous Blur–Oasis rivalry nearly came to blows here.

name: Wilton's Music Hall
description: The world's oldest surviving grand music hall (1858) — 350-cap, deliberately un-restored. Folk, cabaret, chamber music, theatre.
tips: Mahogany Bar open without a ticket. Victorian time capsule.

name: The Hawley Arms
description: Camden pub where Amy Winehouse, Kate Moss, Pete Doherty held court mid-2000s — beer garden, Sunday roasts, music-trivia nights.
tips: Amy-themed photo wall upstairs. Burned down 2008, rebuilt.

name: Royal Opera House
description: Covent Garden's 2,256-seat opera house — world-class Royal Opera and Royal Ballet, with the spectacular glass Floral Hall bar.
tips: Day-seats from £10 — queue from 10am. Tours offered daily.

name: O2 Shepherd's Bush Empire
description: Frank Matcham's 1903 music hall turned 2,000-cap rock venue — intimate for its size, acoustically warm, beloved by artists and fans.
tips: Upper circle has best sight-lines.

name: Rough Trade East
description: Brick Lane's indie record shop-and-venue — in-store gigs from Arctic Monkeys to Florence + The Machine; a London music-fan institution.
address: Dray Walk, 91 Brick Ln, London E1 6QL
tips: Daily free in-store performances — schedule on their website.

name: The Troubadour
description: 1954 Earl's Court coffee-house venue — Bob Dylan's first UK gig (1962), Hendrix open-mic nights, still programming folk and singer-songwriter.
tips: Upstairs café, downstairs venue. Open-mic Wednesdays.
